title: A Biotech Founder Makes the Moral Case for Gene-Editing Human Embryos
gist: Origin Genomics founder Cathy Tie argues gene-editing human embryos is a 'moral imperative' and calls for public funding and new US regulatory pathways, but scientists note base-editing tools still produce unwanted changes, each mutation would be 'a new medicine', and off-target effects cannot be fully ruled out.

insights.claim: Cathy Tie's Origin Genomics, launched in March, plans to bring gene-edited embryos to IVF clinics, and she argues in Trends in Genetics for public funding and new regulatory pathways.
insights.speaker: Kristen V. Brown
insights.so_what: A venture-backed push to commercialize heritable editing signals a nascent, high-risk market.

insights.claim: Tie frames embryo editing as a moral imperative, arguing medicine must prevent avoidable suffering when effective interventions exist, while saying it should not be used to enhance traits like intelligence.
insights.speaker: Kristen V. Brown
insights.so_what: Framing as disease prevention may ease regulatory acceptance.
insights.quote: The obligation of medicine is not only to avoid causing harm but also to prevent avoidable suffering when effective interventions exist

insights.claim: Federal funding for human embryo research is legally restricted in the US, and the FDA is barred from considering clinical trials involving embryos with heritable genetic modifications.

insights.claim: Dozens of countries ban gene editing of human embryos intended for pregnancy, and He Jiankui's 2018 gene-edited babies ended in his imprisonment.
